pages.h1: A severe one-sided headache: a model history
pages.meta_description: Read a structured English headache history covering onset, visual aura, associated symptoms, secondary-headache warning signs, medication use, and functional impact.
pages.patient_card: Ms. Yoon, 28, has had a severe right-sided throbbing headache for 24 hours after seeing flashing lights.

voice.direction: A quiet urgent neurology consultation in clear American English. The doctor is calm, precise, and considerate of light sensitivity. The patient is a 28-year-old woman speaking through significant headache and nausea but remaining natural and intelligible. Keep the pace measured without sounding sedated.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The visual symptoms spread gradually and then cleared. What comparison with earlier headaches should you make next?
The familiar aura and associated symptoms are established, with no focal deficit, fever, or stiff neck. Which secondary-headache context should you screen next?
Frequency, pattern change, acute-medicine use, and general health are clear. Which treatment-relevant background question belongs next?

recall.cue: Ask one question that checks acute-medicine use and possible medication overuse.

source_alignment_notes: The source case supplies the 24-hour right-sided throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, light and sound sensitivity, visual symptoms 30 minutes before pain, similar attacks since adolescence, ineffective ibuprofen, work impact, and desire for rescue treatment.
Negative secondary-headache screens, pregnancy status, allergy status, and attack frequency are author-added draft details and require clinical review before publication.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Ms. Yoon, I'm Dr. Rivera. I can see the light is bothering you, so we'll keep the room dim. Tell me what happened with this headache.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It started yesterday. I saw flashing lights, and about half an hour later I got a strong throbbing pain on the right side of my head.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How did the pain build up?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It became strong over maybe twenty minutes. It wasn't like a sudden explosion.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How severe is it now, and has it let up during the past twenty-four hours?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's about eight out of ten. It eased a little while I slept, but it never fully went away.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Describe exactly what you saw before the pain began.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: There were flickering, flashing spots across my vision. They gradually spread and then cleared after about twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Was that visual experience the same as with your earlier headaches?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes. I've had the same warning before several of my headaches since I was a teenager.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What other symptoms came with this attack?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I feel nauseated, and I vomited twice. Light and ordinary sounds feel unbearable.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had any new weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, or loss of vision?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. The flashing stopped before the pain settled in, and I haven't had any of those other problems.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any fever or a stiff neck?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did this follow a head injury, heavy exertion, or a new medicine? Do you have cancer or a condition that weakens your immune system?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Nothing unusual happened before it started, and I don't have cancer or an immune condition.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How often are these headaches occurring now, and has their usual pattern changed?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Usually once or twice a month. This one feels like my usual attack, but it has lasted longer and has kept me from working.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What have you taken for it, and how often do you use pain medicine in a typical month?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I took ibuprofen yesterday, but it didn't help. I only use it on headache days, usually once or twice a month.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other medical conditions or take any regular medicines?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I'm generally healthy and don't take anything regularly.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: None that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Because pregnancy can affect which causes and treatments we consider, is there any chance you could be pregnant?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, there isn't.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What are you most concerned about, and what help were you hoping for today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I'm worried these attacks will keep disrupting my design work. I'd like something that can stop them when they start.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me summarize. You developed your usual gradually spreading visual warning, followed thirty minutes later by a right-sided throbbing headache with vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound. The attack was not instantly severe, and you report no fever, stiff neck, injury, or new neurologic symptom. It resembles attacks you have had since adolescence, although it has lasted longer and ibuprofen did not help. Have I understood that correctly, and is there anything else I should know?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's correct. I don't think I've left anything out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I'll check your vital signs and perform a focused neurologic examination before we decide what evaluation and symptom relief are appropriate. If the pattern changes suddenly or you develop weakness, trouble speaking, confusion, fever, or a stiff neck, that needs urgent reassessment.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay. That makes sense.

flow: Reduce sensory discomfort and invite the story
Establish onset and time to peak
Characterize the visual symptoms and headache
Compare with prior attacks
Screen for secondary-headache warning signs
Review acute medication and relevant background
Explore work impact and treatment goal
Summarize and give a pattern-change safety net
do_not_miss: Sudden maximal onset or a new, worsening, or substantially changed pattern
Persistent visual loss, weakness, numbness, speech change, confusion, or reduced consciousness
Fever, stiff neck, recent head injury, pregnancy, cancer, or immune suppression
Frequency of attacks and acute-medication use
Functional impact and the patient's goal for rescue treatment

pages.h1: Wheezing during exercise: a model respiratory history
pages.meta_description: Read a patient-friendly English asthma history covering exercise and cold-air triggers, symptom control, severe-attack history, inhaler use, exposures, and patient goals.
pages.patient_card: Ms. Chloe Bennett, 32, develops wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath when she runs outdoors.

voice.direction: A calm respiratory clinic conversation in clear American English. The doctor is attentive and practical. The patient sounds comfortable at rest and concerned but composed. Keep both voices natural and intelligible.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The exercise trigger, timing, reliever response, and weekly frequency are clear. Which control domain should you assess next?
There are no nighttime or resting symptoms and no episode with speech difficulty or reliever failure. Which severe-attack history should you ask about next?
Past severity, inhaler technique, controller use, and exposures are established. Which atopic background or functional goal should come next?

recall.cue: After hearing how the reliever is used, ask one question about ongoing anti-inflammatory or controller treatment.

source_alignment_notes: The source case supplies childhood asthma, childhood eczema, exercise and cold-air triggers two or three times weekly, dry cough, relief within 10 to 15 minutes from a rescue inhaler, no nighttime or resting symptoms, no recent respiratory infection, nonsmoking status, and the patient's safety and treatment concerns.

The public dialogue uses the en-US term 'albuterol' for the source case's salbutamol inhaler. Negative hospitalization, intubation, vaping, workplace exposure, allergy, and family-history details are author-added drafts requiring review.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Ms. Bennett, I'm Dr. Lewis. What would you like us to focus on today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I wheeze and get short of breath when I run, especially outside in cold weather. I'm worried it could turn into a serious asthma attack.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Tell me what you notice first during a run.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Usually a dry cough starts, then my chest feels tight and I hear a whistling sound when I breathe out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How soon does that begin, and what do you do when it happens?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It starts after about ten minutes in cold air. I stop, take my rescue inhaler, and the symptoms settle within ten or fifteen minutes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How many days a week are you needing the inhaler for these symptoms?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Usually two or three days a week, mostly on running days.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do coughing or breathing symptoms ever wake you at night?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I sleep through the night.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What is your breathing like at rest or during ordinary daily activities?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's normal. Walking and work don't bother me.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had a recent cold or noticed another trigger besides running and cold air?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No recent cold. I haven't found a clear trigger indoors.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had an attack where you could not speak in full sentences or the inhaler did not help?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I've always been able to speak, and the inhaler has worked.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever needed an emergency visit, hospital stay, or breathing tube because of asthma?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Nothing that severe.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Which inhaler do you use now? Please walk me through how you use it.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's an albuterol inhaler. I shake it, breathe out, press once while I breathe in, and then hold my breath. I don't use a spacer.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you use any controller inhaler or take any other regular medicine?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No controller and no other regular medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke or vape, or breathe smoke or fumes at home or work?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I don't smoke or vape, my roommate doesn't smoke, and my office doesn't have fumes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have eczema, nasal allergies, or a family history of asthma?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I had eczema as a child. I don't have nasal allergies, and no one else in my family has asthma.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No known medication allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How is this changing your exercise, and what would you like from today's visit?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I've stopped running alone because I'm scared I won't get help. I want to know how well controlled this is, whether I need a controller, and whether my technique is right.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You have cough, chest tightness, wheezing, and shortness of breath after about ten minutes of outdoor running, especially in cold air, on two or three days a week. Albuterol settles it within fifteen minutes. You have no nighttime or resting symptoms and no history of a severe attack, but fear of an attack is limiting your running. Is that accurate, and is there anything else you want me to understand?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's accurate. Being able to run safely is the main thing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Next I'll listen to your lungs, assess your breathing objectively, and watch you use the inhaler. Then we'll agree on an anti-inflammatory treatment and written action plan, including what to do if symptoms worsen or the reliever stops working.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Good. I'd feel better having a clear plan.

flow: Invite the patient's description
Define the exercise pattern and triggers
Measure daytime, nighttime, and activity symptoms
Check severe-attack history
Review reliever response and inhaler technique
Assess smoking, vaping, exposures, and atopy
Explore safety concerns and goals
Summarize and move to objective assessment and an action plan
do_not_miss: Night waking, resting symptoms, and activity limitation
Inability to speak, rapidly worsening breathlessness, or poor reliever response
Previous emergency visits, hospitalization, intensive care, or intubation
Reliever frequency, controller treatment, adherence, and inhaler technique
Smoking, vaping, occupational exposure, and the patient's exercise-safety concern

pages.h1: Thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss: a model history
pages.meta_description: Read a focused English history for new severe thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss, including urgent screening for a hyperglycemic crisis and the patient's treatment concerns.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Choi, 19, has developed severe thirst, hourly urination, fatigue, and an 8-kilogram unplanned weight loss over three weeks.

voice.direction: A same-day endocrine assessment in clear, efficient American English. The doctor is reassuring but appropriately urgent and checks crisis symptoms early. The patient is a tired 19-year-old man who is worried about diabetes and injections, speaking naturally and clearly.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The rapid progression, extreme thirst, and hourly urination are quantified. Which catabolic symptom should you quantify next?
Weight loss and increased appetite are present, without vomiting, abdominal pain, or abnormal breathing. Which remaining crisis sign should you assess next?
Mental status, infection symptoms, prior glucose history, and family history are clear. Which medicine exposure could change the differential?

recall.cue: The patient is hungry despite rapid weight loss. Ask one direct question that screens for an acute hyperglycemic crisis.

source_alignment_notes: The source case supplies the three-week progression, 5 to 6 liters of fluid daily, hourly urination, four or five nighttime trips, increased appetite, 8-kilogram weight loss, fatigue and weakness, no medical history or medication, college setting, nonsmoking status, and fear of injections.

Negative ketoacidosis symptoms, infection symptoms, steroid exposure, allergy status, and family-history details are author-added draft details. The source's available urgent laboratory results are deliberately not revealed during the history-taking transcript.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Choi, I'm Dr. Kim. You look tired, so while we check your vital signs, tell me what has changed.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: For about three weeks I've been incredibly thirsty, going to the bathroom all the time, and losing weight even though I'm always hungry.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How quickly have those symptoms been progressing?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: They've become much worse over the last week. I feel drained and weak now.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: About how much are you drinking in a day?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Five or six liters of water. My mouth still feels dry.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How often are you urinating during the day and overnight?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About every hour, and I wake up four or five times a night.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How much weight have you lost?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Eight kilograms in three weeks. I wasn't trying to lose any.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What has happened to your appetite?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's huge. I eat full meals and feel hungry again soon afterward.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Has your breathing become unusually deep or fast?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, my breathing feels normal.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you felt confused, unusually drowsy, or close to fainting?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I'm exhausted, but I'm thinking clearly and haven't fainted.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any recent fever, infection, or blurred vision?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No fever or infection. My vision gets a little blurry when I'm very tired.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a high blood sugar reading or another major health problem?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I've always been healthy.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does diabetes run in your family?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My grandfather developed type 2 diabetes when he was older. No one else that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you take any prescription medicine, over-the-counter product, supplement, or steroid?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, nothing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: None that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How is this affecting college, and what worries you most about what might be happening?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I can't stay awake in class, and I keep leaving lectures to urinate. I'm worried it's diabetes, and I'm scared that would mean injections every day.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me check that I have this right. Over three weeks you have developed severe thirst, hourly urination including four or five times overnight, increased hunger, fatigue, and an unplanned 8-kilogram weight loss. The symptoms are worsening, but you currently report no vomiting, abdominal pain, unusual breathing, confusion, or fainting. Is that correct, and is there anything else you want to add?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's correct. I mainly want the tests done and to know what happens next.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: These symptoms need prompt assessment today. We'll check your blood sugar and ketones now and do further blood and urine tests as indicated. If you become confused, start vomiting, develop abdominal pain, or breathe deeply and rapidly, we will escalate care immediately. Once we have the results, we'll explain them and discuss any treatment with you rather than assuming what you will need.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Thank you. That helps with the fear.

flow: Assess current appearance while inviting the story
Establish the rapid time course
Quantify fluid intake, urination, and weight loss
Screen immediately for ketoacidosis and dehydration
Check related symptoms and relevant background
Review medicines and steroid exposure
Explore functional impact and fear of injections
Summarize and move to same-day testing
do_not_miss: Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, confusion, drowsiness, or fainting
Degree and speed of weight loss and dehydration symptoms
Recent infection and medications such as glucocorticoids
Family history and prior high glucose readings
The patient's fear of injections without presuming a diagnosis or treatment

sources.title: ADA-led International Consensus — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes

pages.h1: A twisted ankle: a model orthopedic history
pages.meta_description: Read a focused English sports-injury history covering ankle injury mechanism, weight-bearing ability, pain location, neurovascular warning signs, prior injury, and return-to-sport goals.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Jin, 28, has right lateral ankle pain, swelling, and bruising after landing awkwardly during basketball four hours ago.

voice.direction: A focused acute musculoskeletal visit in natural American English. The doctor is concise and systematic about mechanism, weight bearing, and neurovascular safety. The patient is a 28-year-old man in moderate ankle pain who is mainly concerned about fracture and returning to basketball.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The inversion mechanism, rapid swelling, and exact pain location are clear. Which weight-bearing question should come next?
He cannot take four steps, but sensation, color, and temperature are normal. Which injury-severity feature should you assess next?
Open injury, deformity, prior sprain, self-care, and pain behavior are established. Which background or recovery goal belongs next?

recall.cue: He could not take four steps immediately after injury. Ask the separate present-time weight-bearing question.

source_alignment_notes: The source case supplies the four-hour timing, basketball rebound, inward twist, lateral ankle pain, swelling, bruising, painful walking, no significant history or medication, and the patient's concern about fracture and return to basketball.

The ability to take fewer than four steps, absence of deformity or neurovascular symptoms, prior mild sprain, self-care, allergy status, and work impact are author-added draft details requiring review.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Jin, I'm Dr. Parker. Keep the ankle supported while we talk. Walk me through exactly how you injured it.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About four hours ago I came down from a rebound in basketball. My right foot rolled inward, and I fell.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did you feel or hear a pop or crack when it happened?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No crack. I felt a sharp pull on the outside of the ankle.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How quickly did the swelling and bruising appear?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It swelled within minutes. The bruising became obvious over the next couple of hours.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Please point with one finger to where it hurts most.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Right over this outer ankle bone and just below it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Were you able to take four steps immediately afterward?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I managed two steps, then my teammates helped me off the court.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Can you take four steps now, even with a limp?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Putting my full weight on it is too painful.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you noticed any numbness or tingling in the foot?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Has the foot felt cold or looked unusually pale or blue?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. The color and temperature seem normal.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Was there any open wound or an obvious change in the shape of the ankle?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No open cut and no obvious deformity, just swelling.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you injured this ankle before?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I had a mild sprain about three years ago, but it healed completely.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What have you done for it since the injury?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I stopped playing, put ice on it, and kept it raised. I haven't taken pain medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How painful is it while supported, and what makes the pain worse?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's about four out of ten while I keep it still, but it becomes sharp and much worse if I move the ankle or try to stand.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any major medical condition or take any regular medicine?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No medical problems and no regular medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No known medication allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What activities are most important for you to get back to?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I sit at a computer for work, but basketball is what I'm worried about. I want to know whether it's broken and when I can play again.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You rolled the right foot inward four hours ago and developed rapid swelling, bruising, and pain over the outer ankle. You could not take four steps then and still cannot now, but you report no wound, deformity, numbness, or change in foot color or temperature. Is that accurate, and is there anything else I missed?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's all correct.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I'll examine the bones, ligaments, movement, circulation, and sensation. Because you cannot take four steps and have pain near the ankle bone, an X-ray may be appropriate after the examination. We'll protect the ankle now and base return to basketball on the findings and your recovery, not on a fixed date.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay. I appreciate the clear answer.

flow: Reconstruct the landing and direction of force
Establish immediate swelling and pain location
Ask separately about four-step weight bearing
Screen for open injury, deformity, and neurovascular change
Review prior injury and self-care
Identify work and sport goals
Summarize before examination and imaging decision
do_not_miss: Exact mechanism and direction of the twist
Ability to take four steps immediately and during assessment
Point pain over the malleoli and other Ottawa-rule locations during examination
Open wound, deformity, severe pain out of proportion, numbness, or a cold or discolored foot
Prior injury and the patient's functional and return-to-sport goals

pages.h1: A head injury during basketball: a focused emergency history
pages.meta_description: Read a concise English emergency history after a sports-related head injury, prioritizing mechanism, consciousness, memory, neurologic danger signs, bleeding risk, observation, and safe return to play.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Yoon, 20, has headache, dizziness, and mild nausea four hours after a collision during basketball.

voice.direction: A concise emergency department history in clear American English. The doctor is calm, safety-focused, and keeps checking the patient's alertness without sounding alarmist. The patient is a 20-year-old man with mild headache and dizziness who is anxious about brain bleeding and return to sport.

prediction_pauses.prompt: Mechanism, consciousness, memory, and symptom trajectory are established. Which neurologic danger sign should you ask about next?
There is no vomiting, seizure, focal neurologic change, increasing drowsiness, or neck pain. Which bleeding-risk modifier should come next?

recall.cue: After brief confusion without loss of memory, ask one question about how the current symptoms have changed over time.

source_alignment_notes: The source case supplies the four-hour timing, basketball collision, brief disorientation without loss of consciousness, mild throbbing headache, dizziness, nausea, no prior concussion, no medication, and concern about bleeding, imaging, and return to basketball.

Specific collision mechanics, stable symptom trajectory, negative danger signs, absence of neck pain, bleeding risks and substance use, and roommate observation are author-added draft details requiring review.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Yoon, I'm Dr. Adams. We'll keep checking your alertness while we talk. Tell me exactly what happened four hours ago.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Another player and I collided during basketball, and his shoulder hit the side of my head. I fell down and felt dazed.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did you lose consciousness at any point?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I never blacked out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What do you remember from just before and just after the hit?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I remember the play and sitting on the court afterward. My teammate said I seemed confused for about a minute, but I don't have a gap in my memory.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How have the headache, dizziness, and nausea changed since then?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: The headache is still mild, about four out of ten, and hasn't been getting worse. I'm a little dizzy and nauseated.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you vomited or had a seizure?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Since the hit, have you noticed any new problem with vision, speech, strength, feeling, or walking?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Bright light bothers me a little, but I can see, speak, move, and walk normally.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you become more confused or unusually drowsy, or been difficult to wake?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I've stayed awake and feel clearer than I did right after the collision.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have pain or tenderness in your neck?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No neck pain.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I ask because these can change the bleeding risk: do you take a blood thinner, have a bleeding disorder, or use alcohol or drugs before the injury?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No to all of those. I don't take any regular medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a concussion or another significant head injury?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, this is the first time.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: If you go home, who could stay with you and watch for a change?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My roommate can stay with me tonight. I'm worried about a brain bleed and wonder if I need a scan. I also want to know when I can practice again.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You were struck on the side of the head four hours ago and were briefly confused but did not lose consciousness or lose memory. Your mild headache, dizziness, and nausea are not worsening, and you report no repeated vomiting, seizure, new neurologic problem, increasing drowsiness, neck pain, or bleeding risk. Is that correct, and is there anything else I should know?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's correct. Nothing else.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: We'll complete a neurologic and neck examination and use the full findings to decide whether imaging is needed. You must not return to play today. If you go home, your roommate will receive clear written danger signs such as a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, weakness, seizure, or trouble waking you. We'll also give you instructions for classes, driving, follow-up, and a gradual return to sport only after medical clearance.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Understood. I won't go back to practice until I'm cleared.

flow: Confirm current alertness while taking the history
Reconstruct mechanism and timing
Check loss of consciousness and memory
Track symptom severity and direction of change
Screen for neurologic and cervical-spine danger signs
Assess bleeding risk, substances, and prior concussion
Confirm safe observation and patient concerns
Summarize, prohibit same-day return, and give a concrete safety net
do_not_miss: Loss of consciousness, amnesia, confusion, and change in alertness
Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, focal neurologic change, or unequal pupils
Neck pain or tenderness
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, bleeding disorder, and alcohol or drug use
A responsible observer, written return precautions, and no same-day return to play
